title: KEEP MARIJUANA IN TEXAS

updateNote.text:
THE DEADLINE MOVED. On August 8th, hours before leaving for recess, the U.S. Senate passed a stopgap funding bill that incidentally pushed the federal hemp ban back one month: November 12th is now December 11th. The House takes it up when they return from recess in September.

This is a step forward but it was incidental. Nobody acted to delay the ban. How the organization that takes half of everybody's money doesn't have enough funding is beyond me. It is more important than ever before to contact your representatives and reason with them. The 5.5 billion dollars a year THC industry in Texas is still set to be eliminated entirely on December 11th.

Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick is bragging about this, he really believes they are saving Texas. Tens of thousands of locked up citizens, millions of dollars in federal fines, ten thousand bankrupted businesses, 1 in 2 Americans (50% of everybody, 70% of just 18-65 year olds) are on some kind of prescription medication, ketamine is being advertised to children on instagram, and alcohol suicide opioid death rates are at all time highs. Thank you Dan Patrick.

 Visit https://lastprisonerproject.org to see what similar Dan Patrick legislature has accomplished.

description:
On Friday July 31st, every consumable THC product except Delta-9 is being pulled off all Texas shelves, after a 21 day formal notice was published in the Texas Register by the Texas DSHS on July 10th. Come December 11th, the federal reclassification deadline takes the rest: every remaining THC product in Texas, Delta-9 included, is gone. This is a decision that harms Texas more than it helps.

Since 2018 CBD and THC Delta-8 products have entered Texas gas stations, smoke shops, and liquor stores. They now take at least 5 billion dollars annually. This revenue growth in just 8 years almost guarantees it will overtake the alcohol market in Texas at some point. And it should- alcohol is far more dangerous. Any person who consumes these toxins will agree: society is safer with a bottle of willie nelson's tonic than a bottle of jack daniels. There's significantly less aggression, less physical damage of the liver and body, less long term side effects, less pain.

And with a market share like that, it is clear banning these products are not the will of the people. Not by any measure of any kind.

The right solution here is to continue discussion. For the kid who goes to a party for the first time, would you prefer they had THC or liquor? For the veteran seeking pain relief, THC or liquor?

13,701 people die from alcohol every year in Texas alone. Alcohol-related deaths in Texas significantly outpace all drug overdoses combined (which peaked around ~5,500 deaths per year in Texas, with fentanyl accounting for ~1,900). 26.8% of Texas adults report heavy drinking. Deaths related to cannabinoids are extremely rare.

This ban does not aid any of these statistics, it very much worsens the problems we face.

By wiping out a multi-billion dollar legal market overnight, you are not eliminating demand. You are simply forcing consumers back into dangerous alternatives. For some, that means turning to the unregulated illicit street market. For others, it means things worse than weed or alcohol.

I am asking for the decision to be extended to the federal December 11th reclassification deadline.

Letting today's pull stand on such short notice means real businesses lose real wages. A sharp hit against a very young industry for this state, that means real businesses closing down real employees getting fired real people being hurt and displaced.

As I said above, this decision is not the will of the people. The 5 billion dollar market share speaks for itself, and that market doesn't just end. Illegal weed does very very real harm. The cheap illegal vapes, cartridges, and other products being sold send people to the ER frequently. Millions of dollars of new entirely unregulated, untaxed illegal sales, that's just the first month. Second month that illegal market only continues to grow.

A real solution involves FDA regulations, better guidelines (guardrails, not an outright ban), more oversight, more investment. New Mexico is 10 hours away, Arkansas is 5 hours away, Oklahoma is 3 hours away, all of them have massive taxed regulated markets for these products and Texas hands it to them and the multi-billion dollar illegal street dealer scene. For nothing in return.

That is what Friday is about, and I am suggesting to push it to December for now.

By extending this decision to December, Texas businesses stand a far better chance of handling the financial shock of their upfront investments. Over 9,100 licensed hemp retailers and producers across Texas operate in a multi-billion dollar legal industry. Eliminating so many major product lines on a sudden 21-day notice erases 10% to 20% or more of an average storefront's revenue overnight— on top of existing regulatory pressures that have already gutted product inventory. Businesses holding hundreds of thousands of dollars in compliant inventory face catastrophic losses, inventory embargos, and sudden closure. Real people will be fired, dozens of small Texas businesses will shut their doors permanently, and Texas workers will bear the brunt of an unworked timeline.

An extension to the federal December deadline saves real people, and real lives. Please, we implore you to reconsider this.

lawmakers.name: Dan Patrick
lawmakers.title: President of the Senate
lawmakers.counties: All 254 counties. Presides over the full Texas Senate and controls which bills reach the floor.
lawmakers.record: Made banning consumable THC a personal legislative priority and named it SB 3 — the lowest bill number the Senate reserves for the presiding officer’s top priorities. He drove SB 3 through the Senate 24-7 in March 2025, and after Governor Abbott vetoed it, drove SB 5 through 21-8 in the July 2025 special session and SB 6 in the second. Both died in the House. He controls which bills reach the Senate floor, so no delay bill moves without him. The single most important office to persuade.

novContactReps.subject: URGENT CONSTITUENT NOTICE: PROTECT DELTA-9 IN TEXAS BEFORE THE DECEMBER 11TH FEDERAL DEADLINE
novContactReps.body:
Dear Honorable Texas Lawmaker,

I am writing as a concerned Texas voter in the aftermath of the July 31st removal of consumable hemp products from Texas shelves, and in strong opposition to the December 11th federal reclassification that takes the remaining low-dose Delta-9 THC beverages (including 5mg and 10mg products) with it.

On July 31st, every consumable THC product except Delta-9 was pulled off all Texas shelves, on a 21 day formal notice published in the Texas Register by the Texas DSHS. That day has come and gone, and its damage is now landing: over 9,100 licensed hemp retailers and producers across Texas were left holding hundreds of thousands of dollars of suddenly unsellable, fully compliant inventory. Storefronts lost 10% to 20% or more of their revenue overnight. Layoffs and closures have already begun. Come December 11th, the last legal product category — Delta-9 — goes with them, and a $5.5 billion dollar a year Texas industry is finished in a single calendar year.

Since 2018 CBD and THC products built that market across Texas gas stations, smoke shops, and liquor stores, growth that put it on pace to rival the alcohol market in this state. And it should- alcohol is far more dangerous. Society is safer with a bottle of willie nelson's tonic than a bottle of jack daniels. There's significantly less aggression, less physical damage of the liver and body, less long term side effects, less pain.

13,701 people die from alcohol every year in Texas alone. Alcohol-related deaths in Texas significantly outpace all drug overdoses combined (which peaked around ~5,500 deaths per year in Texas, with fentanyl accounting for ~1,900). 26.8% of Texas adults report heavy drinking. Deaths related to cannabinoids are extremely rare. For the kid at their first party, for the veteran seeking pain relief — a precisely dosed, lab-tested 5mg Delta-9 beverage, or liquor?

The July ban did not eliminate demand, and neither will December. It is simply forcing consumers into dangerous alternatives: the unregulated illicit street market, whose cheap untested vapes and cartridges send people to the ER, is now the growth industry in Texas. Every month between now and December that market compounds, untaxed and untested, while New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Arkansas — all with massive taxed, regulated markets — collect the revenue Texas walked away from. For nothing in return.

Delta-9 beverages are the last legal, safest-in-class option left on Texas shelves: precisely dosed, lab-tested, age-gated, and taxed. I am asking you to protect Delta-9 through and beyond the December 11th federal reclassification deadline, and to champion a real solution in its place: FDA regulations, better guidelines, more oversight, more investment — guardrails, not an outright ban.

The July ban emptied the shelves. December 11th decides whether they stay empty forever. Real people, real businesses, and real lives are still on the line. Please, do not let the last domino fall.

contactReps.subject: URGENT CONSTITUENT NOTICE: THE HEMP SHELF PULL LANDS TODAY — EXTEND IT TO DECEMBER 11TH
contactReps.body:
Dear Honorable Texas Lawmaker,

I am writing as a concerned Texas voter to express my strong opposition to the removal of consumable hemp products from Texas shelves that takes effect TODAY, Friday July 31st, and to the December 11th federal reclassification that takes the remaining low-dose Delta-9 THC beverages (including 5mg and 10mg products) with it.

Today is the day it happens: every consumable THC product except Delta-9 comes off all Texas shelves, on just 21 days of formal notice published in the Texas Register by the Texas DSHS on July 10th — and come December 11th, every remaining THC product in Texas, Delta-9 included, is gone. I believe this to be a decision that harms Texas more than it helps.

Since 2018 CBD and THC Delta-8 products have entered Texas gas stations, smoke shops, and liquor stores. They now take at least 5 billion dollars annually. This revenue growth in just 8 years almost guarantees it will overtake the alcohol market in Texas at some point. And it should- alcohol is far more dangerous. Any person who consumes these toxins will agree: society is safer with a bottle of willie nelson's tonic than a bottle of jack daniels. There's significantly less aggression, less physical damage of the liver and body, less long term side effects, less pain.

And with a market share like that, it is clear banning these products are not the will of the people. Not by any measure of any kind.

The right solution here is to continue discussion. For the kid who goes to a party for the first time, would you prefer they had THC or liquor? For the veteran seeking pain relief, THC or liquor?

13,701 people die from alcohol every year in Texas alone. Alcohol-related deaths in Texas significantly outpace all drug overdoses combined (which peaked around ~5,500 deaths per year in Texas, with fentanyl accounting for ~1,900). 26.8% of Texas adults report heavy drinking. Deaths related to cannabinoids are extremely rare.

This ban does not aid any of these statistics, it very much worsens the problems we face.

By wiping out a multi-billion dollar legal market overnight, you are not eliminating demand. You are simply forcing consumers back into dangerous alternatives. For some, that means turning to the unregulated illicit street market. For others, it means things worse than weed or alcohol.

I am asking for the decision to be extended to the federal December 11th reclassification deadline.

Letting today's pull stand on such short notice means real businesses lose real wages. A sharp hit against a very young industry for this state, that means real businesses closing down real employees getting fired real people being hurt and displaced.

As I said above, this decision is not the will of the people. The 5 billion dollar market share speaks for itself, and that market doesn't just end. Illegal weed does very very real harm. The cheap illegal vapes, cartridges, and other products being sold send people to the ER frequently. Millions of dollars of new entirely unregulated, untaxed illegal sales, that's just the first month. Second month that illegal market only continues to grow.

A real solution involves FDA regulations, better guidelines (guardrails, not an outright ban), more oversight, more investment. New Mexico is 10 hours away, Arkansas is 5 hours away, Oklahoma is 3 hours away, all of them have massive taxed regulated markets for these products and Texas hands it to them and the multi-billion dollar illegal street dealer scene. For nothing in return. That is what today is about, and even now an emergency extension matters: I am asking you to push this to December, and to say so publicly before the day is out.

By extending this decision to December, Texas businesses stand a far better chance of handling the financial shock of their upfront investments. Over 9,100 licensed hemp retailers and producers across Texas operate in a multi-billion dollar legal industry. Eliminating so many major product lines on a sudden 21-day notice erases 10% to 20% or more of an average storefront's revenue overnight— on top of existing regulatory pressures that have already gutted product inventory. Businesses holding hundreds of thousands of dollars in compliant inventory face catastrophic losses, inventory embargos, and sudden closure. Real people will be fired, dozens of small Texas businesses will shut their doors permanently, and Texas workers will bear the brunt of an unworked timeline.

An extension to the federal December deadline saves real people, and real lives. Please, we implore you to reconsider this.

contactReps.subject: PETITION: IMPLEMENT NATIVE BROWSER AGE API (ZERO-KNOWLEDGE AGE VERIFICATION STANDARD)
contactReps.body:
To W3C Web Standards Committees, Major Browser Engineers, and Digital Rights Regulators,

I am signing this petition and constituent demand to standardize a privacy-first Browser Age API across modern web browsers.

Every day, internet users are forced to manually enter their birthdates or upload sensitive government IDs to third-party websites just to pass age verification gates. This creates massive honeypots of personal data, exposes users to identity theft, and creates unnecessary friction.

We demand a native, open Browser Age API built directly into web browsers:
1. ONE-TIME VERIFICATION: Users verify their age once in their browser (via Google, Apple Secure Enclave, or Government ID).
2. PRIVACY BY DEFAULT: Websites only receive a cryptographically signed birth year or age-gate boolean (e.g. 18+ / 21+) without accessing exact birth dates.
3. SECURE ZERO-KNOWLEDGE PROOFS: Only high-security institutions (like banks) can request permissioned access to exact month/day/year.
4. CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROOFS: Eliminate third-party tracking while providing verifiable proof of age.

Stop forcing us to re-enter our birthdates everywhere. Add Age to the Browser!

Sincerely,
A Concerned Internet User & Digital Privacy Advocate
